//: Straight-line ABS stop on a uniformly slippery surface (low mu).
//1: Models a hard brake on packed snow / ice.  Friction limit is far
//2: below what the brake hardware can produce — without ABS the wheels
//3: lock instantly and the car slides on whatever-mu, taking forever
//4: to stop.  With ABS the wheels stay near the peak-slip point and
//5: actually decelerate close to the friction limit.  This is the
//6: scenario where ABS earns its keep — stopping distance differences
//9: Lower target speed (15 m/s ≈ 34 mph) because ice + 30 m/s would
//10: take more than max_time_s of coasting before the wheels even
//15: Throttle is capped at 0.16 (not ramped up to 1.0): at mu=0.10 the
//16: front axle's available traction caps out well below what full
//17: throttle demands, so ANY sustained throttle above ~0.16-0.18 rides
//18: past the tire's peak-slip point and the wheel runs away into a
//19: locked-slip spin (measured: 0.20 held flat spikes to |slip|=0.70
//20: within 5 s; 0.16 held flat stays under 0.14 for 20+ s).  Reaching
//21: 15 m/s under a traction-limited 0.16 takes ~48 s (measured) — the
//22: old full-throttle version got there in ~38 s, itself far slower
//23: than the ~3.5 s the original design assumed, because a wheel doing
//24: hundreds of rad/s doesn't translate into vehicle speed.  max_time_s
//25: and the brake-hold window below are stretched to match (was 60 s
//26: total, 7-55 s brake window; now 78 s total, ~50-72 s brake window).
//27: That's a real wall-clock cost increase for this one scenario; see
//28: the PR description for the before/after numbers.
name: abs_low_mu_stop
